solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Shell stuffed with fish and duck

indicators.note: the shell is filled with the fish, so the fish goes inside

parts.note: a pod is the shell of a pea or bean
char is a trout-like fish

explanation.surface: A seafood recipe: a pastry shell filled with fish and duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' sits at the end looking like a second filling, but it is the definition; 'and' merely joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain naming: the pochard is a species of diving duck, the males with a chestnut head.

clue.text: With leader demoted, nation cheers royal with great care

parts.note: SPAIN with its first letter S moved to the back
ta = thanks, cheers
kingly = royal

explanation.surface: A demoted leader watches the nation cheer a royal who treats everyone with great care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demoted' in a down clue means sent lower, so Spain's leading S drops to the bottom. TA is British informal for thanks, which is also what 'cheers' means.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: taking pains over something is taking great care with it.

clue.text: This French saint gets upset over collection of filth

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the earlier pieces sit above the next one

parts.note: ce is French for this
to spit is to show anger, to get upset

explanation.surface: A French saint becomes upset at a heap of rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets upset' looks like an anagram signal, but it is the verb spit, as in 'spitting with rage'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cesspit is a pit for sewage and waste, so literally a collection of filth.

clue.text: Collection artist mounted on beam

indicators.note: in a down clue mounted means raised up, so the letters read upwards, in reverse

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: An art collection by a painter is hung on a wooden beam.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts in London; 'mounted' suggests hanging a picture but signals the upward reading.
explanation.definitionFit: An array is an impressive display or range of things, so it means a collection.

clue.text: Sport in city Den's abandoned: wise man!

parts.note: DRESDEN without DEN
a sage is a wise man

explanation.surface: Someone named Den has left the city to play sport, and a bystander praises his wisdom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Den' looks like a man's name (as in the soap EastEnders), but it is simply the letters to strip from Dresden, the German city.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is the equestrian sport of training a horse to perform precise movements.

clue.text: Draw somersaulting relative next to ring

indicators.note: somersaulting means turning head over heels, so the letters are flipped round

parts.note: pa is a father, a relative
a peal is a ring of bells

explanation.surface: A tumbling family member stands beside a circus ring to attract a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somersaulting' turns PA into AP, followed by PEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Appeal as a noun is attractiveness, the draw or pull something has on people.

clue.text: Hard propping up area towards the rear

indicators.note: in a down clue, what props something up sits beneath it

parts.note: A = area
stern = hard, severe

explanation.surface: Something hard holds up an area at the back of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is written hard-first, but 'propping up' puts STERN below A in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern is a nautical word meaning towards or at the rear of a ship.

clue.text: Part of gospel man is making test of memory

indicators.note: the answer is a part of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'gospel' through 'man is' into the first letter of 'making'

explanation.surface: A test of memory in which someone must recall a passage of the gospel.
explanation.walkthrough: Pelmanism is the card game also called pairs or pelmanism, where face-down cards are turned two at a time; it is named after the Pelman memory-training system.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelmanism is a memory game of matching pairs of face-down cards.

clue.text: Charge city's former university admissions body retrospectively

indicators.note: looking back, so the whole string reads in reverse

parts.note: LA'S: Los Angeles is the city
UCCA, the Universities Central Council on Admissions, since replaced by UCAS

explanation.surface: A city charges its former university admissions body after the fact.
explanation.walkthrough: UCCA was the British body handling university applications until 1993, when it merged into UCAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an accusal, an old word for accusation, is a charge laid against someone.

clue.text: Wearing end to attacks by earnest rebel

parts.note: wearing = in, as in dressed in

indicators.note: take the last letter of the following word

parts.note: last letter of attackS
urgent = earnest, pressing

explanation.surface: A rebel grows weary of the attacks made by an earnest opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' reads as tiring, but it means in, as in someone in a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurgent is a rebel fighting against authority.

clue.text: Cold decoy's sucking lolly

indicators.note: the decoy draws the letter in

parts.note: a lure is a decoy; the 's is 'is'
C = cold, on taps

explanation.surface: A child uses a cold ice lolly as bait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lolly' looks like an ice lolly, but it is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is money, especially ill-gotten; lolly is British slang for money.

clue.text: Poet is beneath hosting Society writers led by editor Mike

indicators.note: to be led by someone is to have them walking in front

parts.note: ED = editor
Mike is M in the phonetic alphabet
under = is beneath
S = society
pens are writers

explanation.surface: A poet feels beneath a society of writers whose meeting is chaired by an editor called Mike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is beneath' looks like part of the surface's grammar, but it is a single piece of wordplay, UNDER, split open to take the society of writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Spenser was the Elizabethan poet who wrote The Faerie Queene.

clue.text: Old soldier sure about crossing river

indicators.note: the reversed word lies across the river, holding it
'about' as in about-turn: YES faces the other way and reads backwards

parts.note: YES (sure) turned round
the Po, Italy's longest river

explanation.surface: A veteran soldier is certain of his route across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as concerning, but it turns YES back to front before PO goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A sepoy was an Indian soldier serving under British or European command.

clue.text: Plant in main island almost meeting fuel total

indicators.note: 'almost' cuts a letter off

parts.note: SARK is what 'island' stands for
gas is a fuel
a sum is a total

explanation.surface: An island running low on fuel tallies the total cost of its main power plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the old poetic word for the open sea, so the definition is a sea plant. 'Plant' and 'fuel' together suggest a power station.
explanation.definitionFit: Sargassum is a brown seaweed that floats in great masses in the ocean, the main.

clue.text: Relate funny turn for trusted friend

indicators.note: funny means odd or peculiar, so the letters are arranged oddly

parts.note: a go is a turn in a game

explanation.surface: Tell an amusing story to a close confidant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funny' rearranges RELATE as ALTERE, followed by GO.
explanation.definitionFit: An alter ego can mean an intimate friend, literally a second self in Latin.

clue.text: Wealthy male curbing European seat of power

parts.note: rich = wealthy
E = European
a stag is a male deer, or a man at a stag party

explanation.surface: A rich man keeps a European out of the seat of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curbing' sits between 'male' and 'European' as if the man is holding back the European, but it is the wealth that does the holding, with the male tacked on after.
explanation.definitionFit: The Reichstag in Berlin houses the German parliament.

clue.text: Poorly splits bit of fish substitute

parts.note: a fin is part of a fish
poorly = ill

explanation.surface: A sick cook botches the filleting of a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Poorly is British for unwell, not badly.
explanation.definitionFit: A fill-in is a person or thing used as a substitute.

clue.text: Item made by man at cafe traveller partly recalled

indicators.note: called back, so read backwards
the answer is part of the words before it

parts.note: the letters start at the T of 'at', run through 'cafe' and stop after TRA of 'traveller', then read right to left

explanation.surface: A souvenir made by a man at a café, which a traveller only half remembers.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards, T-CAFE-TRA gives ARTEFACT. The definition runs on into 'man at' so smoothly that the hiding place seems to start later than it does.
explanation.definitionFit: An artefact is an object made by human hands.

clue.text: Stalin's police chief on centre of quiet peninsula

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the police chief follows the quiet letter
centre of picks the middle letter of quiet

parts.note: the five-letter word whose middle letter is used
Lavrentiy Beria headed Stalin's secret police, the NKVD

explanation.surface: Stalin's secret police boss sits at the heart of a calm peninsula.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' places BERIA after I, the centre of quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Iberia is the peninsula of south-west Europe that holds Spain and Portugal.

clue.text: Bird delayed rival successfully

parts.note: the emu, a large flightless bird
late = delayed

explanation.surface: A bird that got off to a late start still beat its rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rival' is a verb here, as in to match.
explanation.definitionFit: To emulate is to match or equal someone, to rival them successfully.

clue.text: Prudish character simpers dreadfully around knight

indicators.note: the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder
N = knight in chess notation

explanation.surface: A prim woman simpers dreadfully when a knight is around.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess notation a knight is N, since K is taken by the king.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by quality: primness is the prudish character itself, a stiff and proper manner.

clue.text: Bare Trojan hero on film out of position

indicators.note: bare means stripped, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: Hector was the greatest Trojan warrior in the Iliad
pic is short for picture, a film

explanation.surface: A nude Trojan warrior turns up in a film where he does not belong.
explanation.definitionFit: Ectopic is a medical term for something displaced, such as a pregnancy outside the womb, so in the wrong place.

clue.text: Saddo caught lifting antiseptic

indicators.note: in a down clue, the letters are raised so they read upwards

parts.note: a saddo is a loser
C = caught, in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: A sad case gets caught lifting a bottle of antiseptic.
explanation.walkthrough: A saddo is British slang for a pathetic person. 'Lifting' looks like shoplifting, but it turns everything upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Cresol is a coal-tar compound used as an antiseptic and disinfectant.

clue.text: Cowboy losing ring inside of herd: that is clumsiness

indicators.note: losing means giving something up, so the ring letter is removed

parts.note: a gaucho is a South American cowboy
O is ring-shaped

indicators.note: inside of picks the middle letters of herd, leaving off both ends

parts.note: the word whose inner letters are used
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A cowboy, having lost his ring inside the herd, shows how clumsy he is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' is not jewellery here but the round letter O, and 'inside of herd' means its two middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaucherie is awkward, tactless behaviour, from French gauche meaning left-handed, so it means clumsiness.

clue.text: University class on religion that goes over bishop's head

parts.note: MIT, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology
RE = religious education, a school subject

explanation.surface: A university lecture on religion that is too difficult even for a bishop to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes over bishop's head' suggests something beyond his understanding; the definition means it literally. RE is the British school subject religious education.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitre is the tall headdress a bishop wears.

clue.text: Second half of dance perhaps for Joe in LA

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
half of the CHA-CHA, an example of a dance

explanation.surface: The second half of the dance is for someone called Joe who lives in Los Angeles.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe is American slang for coffee, so 'Joe in LA' is coffee in America. 'Perhaps' says the cha-cha is only one example of a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocha is a kind of coffee, and joe is American slang for coffee.

clue.text: Point on back of dry riser?

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the compass point follows the dry letter
back of picks the last letter of dry

parts.note: the word whose last letter is used
east is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A tip about the rear of a dry stair riser.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' puts EAST after Y. Yeast makes dough rise, hence 'riser?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast is a raising agent that makes bread dough rise, so it is cryptically a riser.

clue.text: Pictures from envelopes turned heads

indicators.note: turned means turned round, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: SAEs are stamped addressed envelopes
capes are headlands, also called heads

explanation.surface: Pictures made from envelopes that turned people's heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' changes SAES into SEAS, then CAPES follows. SAE is the British abbreviation for a stamped addressed envelope.
explanation.definitionFit: Seascapes are paintings or photographs of the sea, so they are a kind of picture.

clue.text: Former province began to break up ending in downfall

indicators.note: to break up means to fall apart, so the letters are rearranged
ending in picks the last letter of downfall

parts.note: the word whose last letter is used

explanation.surface: A former province began to split apart, finishing in its downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to break up' rearranges BEGAN as BENGA, then L from the end of downfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Bengal was a province of British India, split in 1947 between India and East Pakistan, now Bangladesh.

clue.text: Hit craft to the left circling key vehicle on track

indicators.note: circling means going round, so the turned pair wraps round the key
in an across answer, going to the left means read backwards

parts.note: to ram is to hit
art is craft or skill
C is a musical key

explanation.surface: A boat is rammed while steering left round an island landmark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the left' sounds like steering the boat, but in an across answer it means read backwards; the key then goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A tramcar is a passenger vehicle running on rails laid in the street, a streetcar.
